newsitem.title: USA: Simpson civil case jury reaches verdicts.
newsitem.headline: Simpson civil case jury reaches verdicts.

text.p: The jury in O.J. Simpson's civil trial reached a verdict on Tuesday afternoon, and court officials said the verdict would be read in open court later in the day.

A decision was reached in the sixth day of jury deliberations, and court spokeswoman Jerrianne Hayslett said the verdict would be announced as soon as the participants in the wrongful-death lawsuit arrived in the courtroom.

Crowds began massing outside the Santa Monica courthouse as the news spread, while police went on a modified tactical alert in case of any disturbances caused by the verdict in what has been dubbed "The Trial of the Century Part Two." Sheriff's deputies hastily erected barriers outside the building to keep potential trouble-makers at bay.

Before it came to a decision in the case, the predominantly white jury of six men and six women listened on Tuesday to four hours of readings of crucial evidence in the case, including Simpson's testimony of his activities on the night his ex-wife and her friend were stabbed to death.

Simpson was acquitted of the June 12, 1994, murders of Nicole Brown Simpson and Ronald Goldman by a criminal jury in October 1995. He then battled a wrongful-death lawsuit brought by the families of the victims.
Should the jurors decide Simpson is responsible for the murders, they will also tell the judge how much the former football star should pay in compensatory damages.

The jury Tuesday also heard readings of the testimony of limousine driver Allan Park, who said he arrived at Simpson's estate at 10:22 p.m. on the night of the murders, but did not see the former football star until 10:55 p.m.
The jury was also read portions of Simpson's testimony regarding a violent argument with his then-wife which occurred on January 1, 1989, and left Nicole Brown Simpson bruised and battered.
In that reading, the jury was reminded that Simpson said he never hit his ex-wife but took "full responsibility" for her injuries.

The panel also heard a reading from the sworn testimony of Simpson's best friend Al Cowlings about how he took Nicole Brown Simpson to the hospital to be treated for her injuries and how she told him that Simpson had beaten her.

Legal analysts said the portions of Simpson's account the jury wanted to hear again -- and their request for a reading of apparently incriminating testimony from Park -- indicated that the panel was leaning in the direction of finding him liable for the deaths.

"It was a bad day for O.J. Simpson on behalf of those jurors who believe that this testimony was meaningful," said well-known Los Angeles trial lawyer Luke McKissack, who has followed the case closely and comments regularly on national television.
"I can't imagine anybody reaching an answer favourable to O.J. Simpson based on (the re-reading of) the testimony we heard today," McKissack added.

The reading of Park's testimony reminded the jurors he said on the witness stand that he arrived at Simpson's mansion at 10:22 p.m. on the night Nicole Brown Simpson and Goldman were murdered, but got no response until about 10:55.

Plaintiffs' attorneys in the civil trial claim Simpson committed the murders about 10:40 p.m. outside his ex-wife's condominium, giving him plenty of time to drive to his home two miles (3 km) away -- a trip that takes four to six minutes -- and be there at 10:55 p.m. when Park saw him.

In the criminal case, testimony from Park, who took Simpson to the airport for an overnight trip to Chicago, was the only one the jury asked to be read to them and the panel reached its not-guilty verdict within minutes of hearing it.

As he did in the criminal trial, Park testified in the civil case that he did not see Simpson's white Ford Bronco parked outside his mansion the night of the murders, as Simpson claimed it was. In addition, he said there were no lights on in Simpson's house when he arrived and they were not switched on until he saw someone going in the door.
The civil case panel heard a reading of Simpson's testimony on what he was doing the night of the murders -- in particular his account of his activities between 9:45 and 11 p.m.
